note: Data-center & generation PPAs. Deals are point-in-time (as of Oct 2026) and will age — treat them as worked examples of structures, not a live deal tracker. Each carries a primary or reputable-trade source. 'level': 1=newcomer, 2=practitioner.

demand.stat: US data-center electricity demand more than doubled (2.3x) from 2018 to 2024 and could reach 325–580 TWh by 2028 — up to roughly 12% of US electricity.
demand.source: LBNL — 2024 US Data Center Energy Usage Report

why: Data centers need large, firm, 24/7 power faster than the grid can build it. 'Speed-to-power' is now the binding constraint — pushing deals toward firm sources (nuclear, geothermal, gas), on-site generation, and direct ownership.

structures.name: Existing-plant nuclear restart / uprate
structures.what: Contract the output of a recommissioned or up-rated existing nuclear unit under a long-term (often ~20-year) PPA.
structures.whyClever: Delivers large, firm, carbon-free baseload that already has an interconnection — far faster than building new generation. Long tenor underwrites the restart capex.
structures.tradeoffs: Limited to the few restartable sites; needs NRC approval; multi-year lead time; can draw scrutiny over keeping the plant off the public grid.
structures.example: Microsoft × Constellation — Three Mile Island Unit 1 (Crane Clean Energy Center)

structures.name: Behind-the-meter co-location
structures.what: Site the data center directly next to a generator and take power on the generator's side of the grid meter, bypassing the transmission network.
structures.whyClever: Fastest path to large firm power — no new transmission, no full interconnection queue. The load and supply are physically married.
structures.tradeoffs: Raises FERC and cost-allocation questions about whether co-located load avoids paying for grid services it still relies on for backup. FERC rejected Talen's amended interconnection agreement for the AWS co-location in Nov 2024.

structures.name: Front-of-meter retail / grid-connected IPP
structures.what: Restructure a co-location deal as a grid-connected, front-of-meter arrangement where the generator becomes the licensed retail supplier to the load.
structures.whyClever: Keeps the commercial relationship and the firm nuclear supply while sidestepping the FERC co-location dispute — the load is a normal grid-connected retail customer.
structures.tradeoffs: The load pays grid charges it avoided under co-location; depends on a retail-choice (deregulated) market.
structures.example: Amazon × Talen — restructured June 2025 (17-yr, up to 1,920 MW)

structures.name: Small modular reactors (SMRs)
structures.what: Sign an offtake for the output of yet-to-be-built small modular reactors, often as a fleet across multiple units.
structures.whyClever: Firm 24/7 carbon-free power that can scale in increments; the corporate offtake gives the developer the demand certainty to build first-of-a-kind units.
structures.tradeoffs: First units are ~2030+; first-of-a-kind cost and schedule risk; needs NRC licensing.
structures.example: Google × Kairos Power (up to 500 MW, first SMR ~2030); Meta × Oklo / TerraPower

structures.name: Enhanced geothermal
structures.what: Offtake firm power from next-generation (enhanced) geothermal projects that engineer heat reservoirs in non-traditional locations.
structures.whyClever: Dispatchable, 24/7 carbon-free power that complements variable solar/wind — fills the firmness gap without nuclear lead times.
structures.tradeoffs: Still scaling; geographically constrained; newer technology risk.
structures.example: Google × Fervo (115 MW, Nevada); Meta × Sage Geosystems / XGS Energy (~300 MW)

structures.name: Bring-your-own-power (on-site generation)
structures.what: Build dedicated on-site generation — typically gas turbines, sometimes fuel cells — to energize the campus directly, ahead of or instead of a grid connection.
structures.whyClever: The fastest route to firm megawatts when the interconnection queue is multi-year. Common among neoclouds racing to deploy GPUs.
structures.tradeoffs: Carbon and air-permit exposure; not carbon-free unless paired with capture or clean fuel; capital and O&M sit with the developer.
structures.example: Crusoe (Stargate / Abilene) — ~29 GE Vernova gas turbines, ~1 GW

structures.name: 24/7 hourly carbon-free matching
structures.what: Procure clean energy so that carbon-free supply matches consumption every hour in every region, rather than netting it out across a year (annual/volumetric matching).
structures.whyClever: A far more rigorous clean-energy claim than annual RECs — it forces procurement of firm and storage resources, not just cheap midday solar.
structures.tradeoffs: Harder and more expensive; some analyses find hourly matching is not always the most cost-effective way to cut system-wide emissions versus targeting dirtier grids.
structures.source: DOE — Clean Energy Resources to Meet Data Center Demand

structures.name: Direct ownership / vertical integration
structures.what: Acquire or co-develop the generation (and sometimes the grid assets) rather than only contracting for its output.
structures.whyClever: Control over the build timeline — the buyer can co-locate generation and data center and move at its own speed instead of waiting on a counterparty.
structures.tradeoffs: Capital-intensive; pulls a tech company into the power business; concentration and execution risk.
structures.example: Google × Intersect Power ($4.75B, Dec 2024) — co-developing generation + data centers

structures.name: Flexible / curtailable load (flexible interconnection)
structures.what: Agree to curtail or shift the data center's consumption during grid peaks in exchange for a faster, cheaper interconnection.
structures.whyClever: Duke's 2025 'Rethinking Load Growth' found the existing US grid could absorb ~76 GW of new load if large users curtail just 0.25% of annual consumption — what the authors call 'curtailment-enabled headroom.' A load willing to flex skips much of the multi-year queue.
structures.tradeoffs: Requires on-site backup or workload scheduling to ride through curtailment; not every AI workload tolerates interruption; still an emerging contracting practice.
structures.example: Duke / Tyler Norris — Rethinking Load Growth (2025); DOE data-center interconnection proposals

structures.name: Frontier offtake (fusion)
structures.what: Sign an early offtake for a not-yet-commercial technology to help finance its first plant.
structures.whyClever: Signals demand and de-risks first-of-a-kind capital; positions the buyer for firm clean power if the technology matures.
structures.tradeoffs: High technology risk; long and uncertain timelines; mostly a strategic bet, not near-term supply.
structures.example: Microsoft × Helion — world's first fusion PPA (~50 MW, target 2028)

caseStudies.title: AWS × Talen — Susquehanna: the co-location fight
caseStudies.participants: Amazon (AWS, buyer) · Talen Energy / Susquehanna Nuclear (seller) · PJM (RTO, filed the ISA) · PPL (transmission owner) · FERC (jurisdiction) · Exelon & AEP (protesting utilities)
caseStudies.load: An AI campus built next to the 2.5 GW Susquehanna nuclear plant, bought by AWS in March 2024, designed to draw hundreds of MW behind the meter and scale toward 960 MW.
caseStudies.gen: Existing dual-unit nuclear — no new generation built. The campus takes a share of a plant that has run since the 1980s.
caseStudies.tnd: The whole dispute was wires. Behind-the-meter co-location bypasses the transmission network, so PJM filed an amended Interconnection Service Agreement to raise the co-located load from 300 to 480 MW. FERC rejected it 2–1 (Docket ER24-2172, Nov 1, 2024): PJM hadn't met the 'high burden' for non-conforming ISA terms, with Chairman Phillips dissenting that a first-of-its-kind configuration deserved one. The rejection froze the BTM expansion and triggered FERC's industry-wide co-location review.
caseStudies.agreement: Original: a BTM power supply arrangement riding on a non-conforming ISA among PJM, Susquehanna Nuclear, and PPL. After the rejection: restructured (June 2025) into front-of-meter retail supply — a 17-year commitment for up to 1,920 MW with Talen acting as AWS's licensed retail electricity provider in Pennsylvania, the load paying full grid charges.
caseStudies.unique: The commercial deal survived but its legal form flipped — from behind-the-meter ISA to front-of-meter retail ESA — because of a docket, not a negotiation. Unlike a VPPA, no strike price or CfD: the contested document was the interconnection agreement itself, and the 'price' of losing was paying transmission charges the structure was built to avoid.
caseStudies.brief: Need: scale a large, firm load beside an operating nuclear plant. Constraint: the preferred behind-the-meter structure depended on a non-standard PJM interconnection agreement.
decisions: Use an existing nuclear site and its established grid position instead of waiting for a new generator.
Start behind the meter so the campus can take plant output without ordinary transmission delivery.
Ask PJM and FERC to expand the non-conforming interconnection agreement from 300 to 480 MW.
After FERC rejected that filing, preserve the supply relationship by moving front of meter and paying grid charges under a 17-year retail arrangement.
caseStudies.failureTest: The replacement structure fails if Talen cannot serve the load as a licensed retail supplier, if the grid cannot support the scale, or if full transmission charges erase the value of the arrangement.
caseStudies.yourTurn: Build a two-column comparison: behind the meter versus front of meter. Price the grid charges, approval path, maximum MW, and schedule in each column before choosing.

history.event: Talen sells the co-located Cumulus campus to AWS; existing ISA allows 300 MW of BTM load.
PJM files the amended ISA to raise co-located load to 480 MW; Exelon and AEP protest.
FERC rejects the amended ISA 2–1 (ER24-2172, 189 FERC ¶ 61,078); Phillips dissents.
FERC opens a show-cause review of PJM's co-located-load rules — the fight goes industry-wide.
Deal restructured front-of-meter: 17 years, up to 1,920 MW, Talen as retail supplier; ~$18B value reported.
FERC finds PJM's tariff unjust and unreasonable for lacking co-location rules (EL25-49) and orders new transmission services for co-located load.

On rehearing (EL25-49-002) FERC keeps the finding, accepts interim NITS plus firm and non-firm contract-demand service for co-located load, and orders more compliance; the same day it issues §206 show-cause orders on large-load interconnection to all six RTOs (EL26-67 to EL26-72).
FERC holds the PJM show-cause docket in abeyance: PJM and its transmission owners must file §205 large-load rules by Nov 16, 2026 or answer the order.

caseStudies.lesson: Interconnection is not paperwork after the deal — it can be the deal. Read the ISA as hard as the PPA, and model the outcome where the regulator makes you pay for the grid you hoped to bypass.

sources.label: FERC order — ER24-2172 (189 FERC ¶ 61,078), Nov 1, 2024
FERC — Chairman Phillips dissent
Utility Dive — FERC rejects the ISA
PowerMag — the $18B front-of-meter restructure
Troutman — FERC's June 18, 2026 co-location rehearing order (EL25-49-002)

glance.supply: Existing 2.5 GW nuclear, nothing new built
glance.contract: BTM interconnection deal rejected, then a 17-year front-of-meter retail ESA
glance.status: FERC wrote co-location rules in EL25-49; PJM's large-load tariff is due Nov 16, 2026

caseStudies.title: Microsoft × Constellation — Crane: the restart PPA
caseStudies.participants: Microsoft (buyer) · Constellation Energy (seller/owner) · NRC (licensing) · DOE Loan Programs Office (~$1B loan) · PJM (interconnection)
caseStudies.load: Microsoft's PJM-region data centers — supply is grid-connected and matched to load across the region, not wired to one campus.
caseStudies.gen: Three Mile Island Unit 1 (835 MW), retired in 2019 for economics, restarted as the Crane Clean Energy Center. ~$1.6B of restart capex, supported by a ~$1B DOE loan; target online 2027, a year ahead of the original 2028 plan.
caseStudies.tnd: Grid-connected — the opposite answer to Susquehanna. By selling into PJM and matching Microsoft's regional load, the deal avoids the co-location fight entirely; the T&D work is reactivating the plant's interconnection, not litigating a new configuration.
caseStudies.agreement: A 20-year, single-buyer PPA for the full output of one unit — price undisclosed. The tenor is the financing: two decades of investment-grade offtake is what makes a nine-figure restart bankable.
caseStudies.unique: Most PPAs finance new construction; this one finances un-retirement. Full-output single-buyer nuclear at 20 years is an outlier against the 12–15-year solar VPPA norm — and there is no CfD mechanic to study, because the point is the block and the balance sheet, not a hub settlement.
caseStudies.brief: Need: a large, round-the-clock carbon-free block for regional data-center demand. Constraint: restarting an existing plant requires long-term revenue, licensing, capital, and a credible delivery date.
decisions: Match a 24/7 load with an existing nuclear unit rather than an intermittent project of the same nameplate size.
Use grid delivery across PJM instead of tying the plant to one campus.
Contract the unit's full output for 20 years so the restart has financeable revenue.
Run the NRC, interconnection, workforce, and financing workstreams in parallel toward the restart date.
caseStudies.failureTest: The PPA cannot make power appear if the NRC approvals, equipment condition, workforce rebuild, financing, or PJM work do not support the target restart date.
caseStudies.yourTurn: Write the buyer's four-item diligence request: restart budget, licensing milestones, interconnection status, and the remedy if commercial operation slips.

history.event: TMI Unit 1 retires — unprofitable in PJM's energy market.
Constellation announces the Crane Clean Energy Center and the 20-year Microsoft PPA.
NRC restart reviews and the workforce rebuild proceed; restart target pulled forward to 2027.
DOE Loan Programs Office closes a $1B loan for the restart, the first time the office finalized a conditional commitment and financial close together.
NRC issues a draft finding of no significant impact for reauthorizing operations and refueling; public comments run to July 8.
Targeted return to service.

caseStudies.lesson: A long-tenor offtake can resurrect firm capacity faster than anything can be built new. When you can't co-locate, buy the block and let the grid deliver it.

glance.load: Microsoft's PJM-region data centers, matched across the grid
glance.supply: Three Mile Island Unit 1 restart, 835 MW nuclear
glance.status: $1B DOE loan closed Nov 2025; NRC draft finding Jun 2026; restart targeted 2027

caseStudies.title: Meta × Entergy — Louisiana: the regulated-utility build
caseStudies.market: MISO South · Richland Parish, LA (vertically integrated state)
caseStudies.participants: Meta (customer) · Entergy Louisiana (utility, builds and owns) · Louisiana PSC (approves) · settlement signatories incl. LPSC staff, Walmart, Sierra Club, Southern Renewable Energy Association · Louisiana consumer advocates (opposing)
caseStudies.load: Hyperion — Meta's largest data center, a Richland Parish campus first planned at 2,000–2,500 MW and now described at roughly 5 GW as it ramps.
caseStudies.gen: Entergy builds and rate-bases three combined-cycle gas plants totaling 2.26 GW — two in Richland Parish (online late 2028), one at the existing Waterford site — plus contracted solar additions. Meta doesn't sign a PPA with a developer; it takes utility service from new-build generation.
caseStudies.tnd: The utility also builds the delivery: new substations and transmission approved in the same proceeding. Because Louisiana is vertically integrated, generation, wires, and the service agreement all run through one docket at the Louisiana PSC.
caseStudies.agreement: A 20-year electric service agreement under Entergy's tariff, with terms designed to shield other ratepayers — Meta commits to pay for the plants built for it. Approved 4–1 by the LPSC in August 2025 as a settlement; opponents argued the utility bypassed competitive solicitation.
caseStudies.unique: There is no PPA at all. The 'negotiation' is a regulatory proceeding: intervenors sign the settlement, the commission votes, and counterparty protections live in the tariff rather than in bilateral credit annexes. This is the default path for gigawatt loads across the vertically integrated South and Midwest.
caseStudies.brief: Need: serve a 2,000–2,500 MW campus in a vertically integrated utility territory. Constraint: Meta cannot choose a retail supplier, and new plants and wires require commission approval and ratepayer protection.
decisions: Use the incumbent utility rather than a direct developer PPA because Louisiana does not offer the needed retail path.
Plan generation, substations, transmission, and the campus ramp in one service case.
Put the long-term payment obligation into an ESA and tariff terms so the dedicated build does not fall on other customers.
Obtain approval through a contested LPSC proceeding and settlement before construction.
caseStudies.failureTest: The program stalls if the commission rejects cost recovery, the load commitment does not cover dedicated investment, or generation and transmission miss the campus ramp.
caseStudies.yourTurn: Draft three protections for existing ratepayers and three protections Meta would ask for if the utility misses an energization milestone.

history.event: Entergy announces it will serve Meta's Richland Parish campus; files for three CCGTs.
Contested proceeding: consumer advocates challenge need, bidding, and ratepayer risk.
LPSC approves the settlement 4–1.
Groundbreaking on the first Richland Parish plant; the LPSC adopts 'Lightning' fast-track rules that skip the market test when a customer funds most of a dedicated build.

Entergy files a second application (Docket U-37882): seven more combined-cycle units (~5.2 GW), 2,500 MW of solar, three battery projects, roughly 250 miles of transmission and nuclear uprates, about $12.9B, recovered from Meta through a contribution-in-aid-of-construction agreement.
LPSC approves the expedited schedule 4–1; Commissioner Lewis dissents over the lack of competitive bidding.
Evidentiary hearing on the second build; a final vote is expected around December 2026. First Richland Parish units from the 2025 approval remain targeted for late 2028.

caseStudies.lesson: In regulated states the energy lead's counterparty is a commission as much as a company. The winning skill is the docket — settlement coalitions, ratepayer-protection terms, and timeline discipline through a contested case.

caseStudies.title: Crusoe — Abilene (Stargate): the energy-park hybrid
caseStudies.market: ERCOT · Lancium Clean Campus, Abilene, TX
caseStudies.participants: Crusoe (developer/operator) · Lancium (energy-park developer, holds the interconnection) · OpenAI / Oracle (Stargate tenants) · Microsoft (900 MW AI-factory tenant) · GE Vernova (turbine supply) · Engine No. 1 & Chevron (gas JV partners)
caseStudies.load: The flagship Stargate campus: eight buildings and 1.2 GW in phase two, four buildings operational by March 2026, plus a further 900 MW AI-factory campus for Microsoft — 2.1 GW on one site.
caseStudies.gen: A stack, not a contract: ~29 GE Vernova gas turbines (~1 GW) on site for speed and backup, behind-the-meter solar and batteries, a separate Crusoe × Engine No. 1 × Chevron JV assembling 4.5 GW of gas for AI campuses, and proximate West Texas wind.
caseStudies.tnd: Both answers at once. Lancium's energy park holds a 1.2 GW ERCOT grid interconnection — among the largest load connections in the market — while the on-site turbines energize buildings before and beside it. ERCOT's energy-only market and its new ≥75 MW large-load process are the backdrop.
caseStudies.agreement: No headline PPA. The 'contract stack' is turbine supply and EPC agreements, the park's interconnection agreement, land/energy-park arrangements with Lancium, tenant leases with OpenAI/Oracle/Microsoft, and JV agreements for the gas fleet. Ownership replaces offtake.
caseStudies.unique: Inverts the corporate-PPA model completely: instead of contracting a developer's electrons at a strike price, the operator becomes the generator. Speed is the strike — turbines on pads beat queue positions — and the exposure is fuel, permits, and carbon rather than basis and shape.
caseStudies.brief: Need: energize a multi-gigawatt campus in phases faster than a single grid or generation project can arrive. Constraint: the load, interconnection, turbines, tenants, and fuel arrangements have different schedules and counterparties.
decisions: Choose an energy park that already controls a large ERCOT load interconnection.
Add on-site gas turbines so early buildings do not wait for the full grid ramp.
Layer solar, batteries, wind, and a larger gas venture around the grid and turbine base.
Use ownership, equipment, EPC, land, tenant, interconnection, and joint-venture contracts rather than one PPA.
caseStudies.failureTest: The campus misses its date if the grid ramp and on-site plant both slip, or if fuel, air permits, turbine delivery, and tenant obligations are not managed as one critical path.
caseStudies.yourTurn: Draw the contract stack and put one accountable owner beside each interface: grid, turbines, fuel, site, tenants, and clean-energy supply.

history.event: Crusoe breaks ground at the Lancium Clean Campus in Abilene.
GE Vernova turbine orders scale on-site generation toward ~1 GW; Stargate names Abilene its flagship.
Crusoe, Engine No. 1, and Chevron unveil a 4.5 GW gas venture for AI data centers.
Phase two begins: eight buildings, 1.2 GW, backed by the park's grid interconnection plus BTM solar and storage.
First ~200 MW phase energized with Oracle as anchor tenant; permit filings show the first on-site turbines (~360 MW) alongside the grid tie.
Four buildings operational; new 900 MW Microsoft AI-factory campus announced with its own on-site plant.

caseStudies.lesson: At the frontier, the energy lead's job stops being 'sign a PPA' and becomes 'assemble a power company' — interconnection rights, turbines, fuel, and renewables under one campus roof.

caseStudies.title: xAI — Colossus, Memphis: speed vs. social license
caseStudies.market: TVA territory · Memphis, TN (federal utility — outside FERC rate jurisdiction)
caseStudies.participants: xAI (owner) · Memphis Light, Gas & Water (municipal utility, TVA's largest customer) · TVA (wholesale supplier; board approves large loads) · Shelby County Health Department (air permits) · SELC and South Memphis residents (opposing)
caseStudies.load: The Colossus supercomputer, stood up in months inside a former appliance factory — grid demand of 150 MW growing by another 150 MW, alongside self-supplied turbines — and a second site, Colossus 2, powered from a turbine plant across the state line in Southaven, Mississippi.
caseStudies.gen: Grid supply from MLGW/TVA plus dozens of mobile gas turbines on site. The July 2025 air permit covers 15 turbines (~247 MW) through January 2027; reporting and aerial imagery identified roughly 35 units on site, and residents allege months of unpermitted operation.
caseStudies.tnd: TVA is a federal power authority — its board, not FERC or a state PUC, approves serving large new loads, and MLGW delivers. Grid approvals (Nov 2024, then +150 MW) came fast; the binding process turned out to be county air permitting and community opposition in a neighborhood with a long pollution history.
caseStudies.agreement: A municipal power supply agreement (MLGW service backed by TVA board-approved wholesale supply) plus self-owned BTM generation under county air permits — no corporate PPA anywhere in the stack.
caseStudies.unique: Shows the non-contract constraints that no PPA clause can fix: permits, environmental-justice opposition, and a utility governance path (TVA board votes) that most playbooks ignore. The 'counterparty' that can stop the campus is the community.
caseStudies.brief: Need: energize a fast-built computing campus in months. Constraint: utility supply was limited at first, while on-site turbines required air permits and affected a community with an existing pollution burden.
decisions: Reuse an existing industrial site to shorten the building schedule.
Combine MLGW/TVA grid service with mobile on-site generation rather than wait for one source to cover the load.
Seek TVA board approval for the grid increments and county permits for the turbines.
Continue expanding while environmental groups and residents challenge the permit and operating record.
caseStudies.failureTest: Fast electrical work does not secure the site if air permits, monitoring, public-health impacts, or community consent can stop or constrain the turbines.
caseStudies.yourTurn: Rebuild the original critical path with permitting and community engagement before turbine deployment. Name the evidence required at each gate.

history.event: xAI picks Memphis; Colossus goes live in ~122 days with turbines self-supplying much of the load.
TVA board approves 150 MW of grid supply via MLGW.
SELC petitions over unpermitted turbines; aerial imagery shows ~35 units against 15 later permitted.
Shelby County issues an air permit: 15 turbines, ~247 MW, expiring January 2027.
27 turbines are installed and run in Southaven, MS to power Colossus 2 before any state air permit, per the later complaint; TVA approves a further 150 MW for Memphis.
Mississippi DEQ grants an air permit for the 27 Southaven turbines; the NAACP says the state moved too fast.
NAACP (SELC and Earthjustice) sues xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech under the Clean Air Act in federal court; a preliminary-injunction motion follows May 6, and groups appeal the permit.

caseStudies.lesson: Speed-to-power has a social bill. An energy lead who wins the megawatts but loses the neighborhood has not secured the site — permit strategy and community engagement belong in the power plan.

caseStudies.title: AEP Ohio — the tariff that wrote the terms
caseStudies.market: PJM · central Ohio (Columbus 'data center alley'), distribution tariff at the Ohio PUCO
caseStudies.participants: AEP Ohio (utility) · PUCO (regulator) · Ohio Consumers' Counsel and PUCO staff (settlement signatories) · data-center and hyperscale intervenors (Google, Amazon, Microsoft among parties) · appeal pending at the Ohio Supreme Court
caseStudies.load: Not one campus but a class: ~30 GW of central-Ohio data-center service requests against a system built for a fraction of that — the queue that forced a rule.
caseStudies.gen: None directly — this case is pure wires and terms. Generation is procured separately in PJM; the tariff governs how the distribution utility must be paid for serving very large new loads.
caseStudies.tnd: AEP Ohio faced billions in transmission and distribution buildout for loads that might never materialize. The PUCO-approved tariff makes new large data centers pay for at least 85% of contracted capacity for up to 12 years — whether or not they draw it — with exit fees, before the wires get built.
caseStudies.agreement: Not a bilateral contract: a class tariff (Case No. 24-508-EL-ATA, approved July 9, 2025) that functions as the standard-form ESA every new large load must sign. The 'negotiation' happened once, in a settlement among the utility, staff, and consumer advocates.
caseStudies.unique: The inverse of every other case: no buyer and seller shaking hands, but a regulator writing default contract terms for an entire customer class. Its 85%/12-year ratchet became the reference point other states now copy — the market's minimum-take clause is being drafted in dockets, not deal rooms.
caseStudies.brief: Need: decide which large-load requests are firm enough to justify billions in grid investment. Constraint: roughly 30 GW of requests included projects that could withdraw after the utility built for them.
decisions: Treat speculative load as a portfolio risk to the utility and its existing customers, not only as bilateral credit risk.
Create one data-center customer class instead of negotiating a different minimum-take term for every campus.
Use an 85% minimum demand obligation, a term of up to 12 years, and exit provisions to test commitment.
Set the commercial rule through a PUCO tariff case and settlement, with appeals handled in the regulatory process.
caseStudies.failureTest: The tariff misses its purpose if obligations are too weak to cover stranded upgrades, or so rigid that financeable projects leave the territory instead of committing.
caseStudies.yourTurn: For a campus that ramps 100, 300, 600, then 900 MW, compare the bill under an 85% ratchet with actual use and identify the hardest year to finance.

history.event: AEP Ohio files data-center tariff provisions after central-Ohio requests approach 30 GW.
Settlement reached with PUCO staff, the Consumers' Counsel, and others; hyperscalers litigate terms.
PUCO approves the settlement — ≥85% minimum demand for up to 12 years, with exit provisions.
PUCO denies rehearing sought by the hyperscalers and the Ohio Manufacturers' Association; in November the OMA appeals to the Ohio Supreme Court.
AEP reports central-Ohio requests fell from about 30 GW to roughly 5.7 GW once the minimum-bill and exit terms applied.

The ratchet travels: Minnesota approves Xcel's large-load tariff (May 15, 15-year term), New Jersey signs the Data Center Fair Share Act (Jul 7, 85% for 10 years), and Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Virginia adopt their own versions.

caseStudies.lesson: Watch the tariff dockets as closely as the deal flow: the ratchets, terms, and exit fees an energy lead will face were set in a case they may never have heard of.

caseStudies.title: Google × Fervo — Cape Station: the firm PPA with an option
caseStudies.market: Utah · Beaver County (PacifiCorp territory); grid delivery, with Utah's SB132 opening a direct-to-load route
caseStudies.participants: Google (buyer; also a 2025 Series E investor) · Fervo Energy (developer and seller) · Cape Station GeoCluster, Beaver County, UT · Utah regulators (direct-to-load approvals) · earlier: NV Energy (115 MW Clean Transition Tariff deal, 2024)
caseStudies.load: A potential Google data center in Utah. Fervo calls the PPA its foundational power block, while the site itself still depends on engineering feasibility, state and local approvals, and commercial conditions.
caseStudies.gen: Enhanced geothermal: horizontal wells drilled into hot dry rock feed binary-cycle plants that run around the clock. Cape Station's first ~100 MW phase (three 33 MW GeoBlocks) reached first power on Sep 24, 2026 and declared its first block in commercial operation on Sep 30, 2026. Fervo is extending the GeoCluster with repeatable GeoBlocks beyond that phase and the earlier SCE and Shell contracts; Google's 396 MW is expected online in 2028.
caseStudies.tnd: Front of meter: Cape Station interconnects into the Utah grid and the output is scheduled to Google's load, the conventional offsite route. Utah's 2025 SB132 lets a large customer contract directly with a generator subject to regulatory approval, which Fervo names as a possible path.
caseStudies.agreement: A 396 MW PPA signed Sep 1, 2026, price and tenor undisclosed (trade coverage reports 15 years delivered in four 99 MW tranches from Q3 2028), plus an option for Google to add about 600 MW by June 2030, taking the total to nearly 1 GW. The deal lifts Fervo's portfolio past 1 GW of binding PPAs.
caseStudies.unique: This is the closest case to a textbook PPA — one buyer, one project, a fixed block — but it buys clean-firm output rather than shaped solar, and the headline term is an option: a right, not an obligation, to more than double the block as the campus and the resource prove out. The buyer pays for flexibility instead of carrying basis.
caseStudies.brief: Need: a firm, carbon-free block for a Utah campus that may or may not be built at full size. Constraint: enhanced geothermal is new at scale, so the buyer wants exposure to the resource without committing the whole campus up front.
decisions: Pick a clean-firm resource that runs around the clock instead of a larger intermittent nameplate that leaves night-time holes.
Buy from a developer with an operating record — Project Red in Nevada since 2023 and the 115 MW NV Energy tariff deal — before committing 396 MW.
Size the firm commitment to the 2028 tranche and hold a ~600 MW option to June 2030 rather than contracting the full gigawatt now.
Keep delivery front of meter through the utility grid, with Utah's direct-to-load statute as a fallback route.
caseStudies.failureTest: The deal underdelivers if drilling or plant performance slips the 2028 tranche, if the Utah campus is not approved, or if the option lapses before both the resource and the load are proven.
caseStudies.yourTurn: Price the option: list what Google gives up by waiting until 2030 (price, queue position, tranche timing) against what it avoids by not contracting 1 GW on day one.

history.event: Project Red, Fervo's Nevada commercial pilot, comes online and supplies the grid serving Google's Nevada data centers.
Fervo, Google and NV Energy sign a 115 MW PPA under Nevada's new Clean Transition Tariff.
396 MW Cape Station PPA signed, with a ~600 MW expansion option to June 2030; Fervo's shares jump on the news.
Cape Station achieves first power in Beaver County, Utah.
First 33 MW GeoBlock declared in commercial operation ahead of schedule; further GeoBlocks follow toward the 2028 deliveries.

caseStudies.lesson: When the resource is new, buy the proven tranche and option the rest. A clean-firm PPA with a dated expansion right turns a technology bet into a staged commitment both sides can finance.

caseStudies.title: NIPSCO × Amazon — Indiana: the PPA inside the utility
caseStudies.market: MISO · northern Indiana (LaPorte County), vertically integrated; IURC Cause No. 46322
caseStudies.participants: Amazon Data Services (customer, with a guaranty from its ultimate parent) · NIPSCO (regulated utility, retail seller) · NIPSCO Generation LLC, 'GenCo' (non-regulated affiliate that builds and owns) · IURC (approves) · OUCC, NIPSCO Industrial Group and LaPorte County (settling parties) · Citizens Action Coalition (opposing)
caseStudies.load: Amazon data centers in northern Indiana energizing from Jan 1, 2027 and ramping to as much as 2,400 MW by the end of 2032.
caseStudies.gen: GenCo builds roughly 3,000 MW of new dispatchable capacity for 2,400 MW of load — combined-cycle gas at the Schahfer site plus battery storage, approved in a companion order — sized with a reserve margin and spare capacity that can support the wider grid.
caseStudies.tnd: Two contracts chained through the utility: GenCo sells the plants' output to NIPSCO under a PPA (GenCo makes the MISO and FERC filings), and NIPSCO serves Amazon at retail under a 15-year special contract. New transmission to the campus is built by NIPSCO and paid for under that contract rather than by other customers.
caseStudies.agreement: Customer Contract dated Sep 18, 2025: 15 years from Jan 1, 2027, a fixed capacity charge plus pass-through energy and 'Shared System Charges', a parent-company guaranty, termination rights with termination payments, and — per the filing — a one-time right to cut the commitment by up to 1,200 MW by March 2029. The IURC approved the contract, the GenCo PPA, the settlement and both alternative regulatory plans on June 17, 2026.
caseStudies.unique: A PPA appears here, but neither party to it is the data center: it is an inter-affiliate contract between a utility and its unregulated generation arm, built so the plants never enter NIPSCO's general rate base. Other customers are shielded by contract rather than by tariff and receive about $1B of bill credits over 15 years — the mirror image of the rate-based Entergy build.
caseStudies.brief: Need: serve a 2,400 MW ramp in a vertically integrated state without putting 3,000 MW of new plant on other ratepayers. Constraint: Indiana lets the utility sell retail, but a dedicated build at that scale needs a structure the commission and consumer advocates will accept.
decisions: Create a non-regulated affiliate (GenCo) to own the dedicated generation, keeping it out of the general rate base.
Chain the supply through a PPA from GenCo to NIPSCO, so the utility stays the retail seller while plant risk sits in the affiliate.
Fix Amazon's obligation in a 15-year special contract: capacity charge, parent guaranty, termination payments and a dated downsizing right.
Settle with the consumer counselor and industrial customers by crediting other ratepayers for shared-system use before the commission vote.
caseStudies.failureTest: The structure fails if the GenCo plants slip past the 2027–2032 ramp, if Amazon exercises the 1,200 MW cut and the surplus capacity cannot be sold, or if FERC or MISO reject the affiliate PPA's terms.
caseStudies.yourTurn: Map the three contracts (Amazon–NIPSCO, NIPSCO–GenCo, GenCo–MISO/FERC) and mark which party holds construction risk, fuel risk and load-loss risk in each.

history.event: NIPSCO and Amazon Data Services sign the Data Center Customer #1 special contract.
NIPSCO and GenCo file the joint petition (Cause 46322): special contract, GenCo PPA, alternative regulatory plans and depreciation rates.
Settlement with the OUCC, the NIPSCO Industrial Group and LaPorte County; Citizens Action Coalition opposes.
IURC approves the settlement, special contract and PPA; a companion order approves GenCo's gas and battery resources; NiSource cites about $1.4B of customer savings.
Scheduled: energization begins and load ramps toward 2,400 MW by end-2032, with GenCo's affiliate PPA filed at MISO/FERC.

caseStudies.lesson: In a regulated state the PPA can live inside the utility. Where the plant sits on the org chart decides who carries it, so read the affiliate contract and the settlement as closely as the customer contract.

caseStudies.title: PJM — the reliability backstop: when the market writes the contract
caseStudies.market: PJM (13 states + DC) · FERC Dockets ER26-3380 and EL26-108
caseStudies.participants: PJM (filed the procurement) · FERC (accepted and suspended it) · PJM Board and the 13 governors' 'Statement of Principles' states · Data Center Coalition and electric distributors (rival design) · consumer advocates and the Ohio Consumers' Counsel (protesting) · PJM Settlement, Inc. (counterparty for buyers)
caseStudies.load: Not one campus but the region's forecast. Large loads drove the 2028/29 Base Residual Auction 6,831 MW short of the reliability requirement; it cleared at the $325/MW-day cap on Jul 14, 2026 ($16.4B, against $29.7B without the collar), after the 2027/28 auction had already cleared 6,623 MW short.
caseStudies.gen: Whatever new capacity can commit: the Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBP) would buy up to 15-year commitments from new resources, from the 2028/29 through the 2042/43 delivery year, in a pay-as-bid auction. The target is cut by documented bilateral contracts and self-supply serving new load and by distributors that opt out.
caseStudies.tnd: The wires here are market rules. PJM proposed to allocate the target, and the cost, to each distribution zone by its share of forecast load growth, so zones adding data centers pay. FERC found that allocation, the transmission-owner exit rules and the LSE collateral requirements not shown to be just and reasonable, and set a paper hearing on them.
caseStudies.agreement: No bilateral PPA: tariff Attachment DD §18 — a one-time procurement with PJM Settlement as the buyers' counterparty, a must-offer into later capacity auctions as a price-taker, and (in the Board's version) a $555/MW-day cap on the average accepted offer. Filed Jul 31, 2026; accepted but suspended five months on Sep 29, 2026, effective Feb 28, 2027, subject to refund; initial briefs due 45 days after the order unless PJM refiles.
caseStudies.unique: The counterparty is the market itself. A buyer that brings new generation under a signed contract of five or more delivery years nets out of the target; one that does not pays its zone's share of a 15-year commitment it never negotiated. In a capacity market a data center's PPA is also a defense.
caseStudies.brief: Need: get new capacity built for a 2028 shortfall that two auctions failed to close. Constraint: a one-off, long-term procurement must pass FERC's just-and-reasonable test, with the cost landing on the loads that caused it rather than on everyone.
decisions: Replace a failed one-year auction signal with up to 15 years of price certainty for new resources, the term the governors' principles asked for.
Run a bilateral matchmaking track alongside the auction so loads and developers can contract directly and shrink the central target.
Credit bilateral contracts and self-supply against the target so loads that bring their own generation are not charged twice.
Allocate the remaining cost by zonal load growth with hard LSE collateral, then defend it at FERC, which kept the design but reopened those three terms.
caseStudies.failureTest: The backstop fails if the suspension and paper hearing push the auction past the point where 2028/29 resources can be built, if cost allocation lands on zones without new load, or if collateral rules keep load-serving entities and cooperatives out.
caseStudies.yourTurn: For a 500 MW campus in a PJM zone, estimate what it would owe under a zonal load-growth allocation, then show how a signed five-delivery-year contract for new capacity changes that number.

history.event: The 2027/28 BRA clears 6,623 MW short at its $333.44/MW-day cap — the first auction in PJM history to miss the reliability requirement.
The White House energy council and all 13 PJM governors publish principles asking PJM for 15-year price certainty and a backstop auction by September 2026.
Stakeholders endorse a $555/MW-day data-center backstop; PJM runs a bilateral matchmaking RFP (responses Jul 21). On Jul 14 the 2028/29 BRA clears 6,831 MW short at the $325 cap.
The PJM Board adopts the RBP with opt-outs, the $555 cap and LSE collateral; PJM files at FERC (ER26-3380), supplemented Aug 14.
FERC accepts the RBP, suspends it five months to Feb 28, 2027, opens a paper hearing and a §206 proceeding; Chairman Swett's concurrence faults the last-day filing. PJM cancels the Sep 30 bid window.

caseStudies.lesson: In a capacity market the deal you did not sign still bills you. Track the auction and the backstop like a contract: bring your own new supply under a long contract and you net out; wait, and the market assigns you a 15-year obligation.

vppCases.title: NRG × Renew Home × Google Cloud — the retail thermostat fleet
vppCases.market: ERCOT · Texas retail (NRG brands incl. Reliant)
vppCases.participants: NRG (retail provider, dispatches) · Renew Home (Google Nest spin-out; devices and enrollment, co-funds up to $150/customer acquisition) · Google Cloud (AI dispatch platform) · enrolled households (the 'plant')
vppCases.load: Hundreds of thousands of Texas homes — the target is a ~1 GW VPP by 2035, capacity equivalent to about 200,000 homes at peak.
vppCases.gen: No generator. Capacity comes from Vivint and Nest smart thermostats (installed free for eligible retail customers) shifting HVAC load before and through peaks, orchestrated by AI dispatch on Google Cloud. Rollout began spring 2025.
vppCases.tnd: Interconnects nowhere: the resource lives behind thousands of distribution meters and shows up as load that doesn't materialize. In energy-only ERCOT, that peak-hour absence is worth roughly what a peaker's output earns — and it frees headroom the large-load queue is fighting over.
vppCases.agreement: A partnership and enrollment stack instead of a PPA: NRG × Renew Home commercial agreement (device co-funding, exclusivity on new Nest demand-response enrollments in Texas), per-household enrollment terms bundled into retail plans, and dispatch rights exercised by the retailer.
vppCases.unique: Against a classic PPA: no COD, no nameplate, no settlement point. 'Volume' is a statistical forecast of fleet response, revenue is avoided supply cost and market position rather than a strike price, and the counterparty is a churn-prone consumer base recruited $150 at a time.

history.event: NRG, Renew Home, and Google Cloud announce the ~1 GW-by-2035 Texas VPP partnership.
Enrollment opens across NRG retail brands; free professional thermostat installs begin.
Fleet scales through summer peaks; DOE's Liftoff analysis pegs national VPP potential at 80–160 GW by 2030.

vppCases.lesson: A VPP 'PPA' is really a customer-acquisition machine with dispatch rights. The scarce asset isn't steel — it's enrollment, retention, and trustworthy fleet statistics.

vppCases.title: Sunrun — CalReady & PG&E: batteries as seasonal capacity
vppCases.market: California · CAISO footprint, state grid-support program + PG&E's 2025 SAVE VPP
vppCases.participants: Sunrun (aggregator; owns/leases the systems) · ~56,000 customer households (~75,000 batteries) · California's state grid-support program (pays for capacity) · PG&E (local dispatch under the SAVE VPP) · CAISO (the grid it relieves)
vppCases.load: A fleet, not a campus: 75,000 residential solar-charged batteries — quadruple the prior year — expected to deliver up to ~250 MW during two-hour peak events.
vppCases.gen: Stored rooftop solar, discharged on command. CalReady stands ready 4–9 p.m., May through October; the Local PeakShift Power fleet under PG&E's SAVE program dispatched 50+ times for 1,200+ dispatching hours from July to October 2025 into constrained local areas.
vppCases.tnd: The T&D story runs backward: instead of building wires to deliver power, the batteries sit past the constraint and inject exactly where distribution feeders run hottest — capacity that arrives in months, targeted at circuits, with zero transmission build.
vppCases.agreement: Seasonal capacity contracts, not energy sales: program payments per enrolled battery (customers earn up to ~$150 per battery per season), pay-for-performance against dispatch windows, and measurement-and-verification baselines standing in for a meter at a plant gate. FERC Order 2222 opens the parallel wholesale path for such aggregations.
vppCases.unique: Against a classic PPA: the seller doesn't own a plant — it marshals tens of thousands of customer systems; 'availability' is a fleet statistic; the product is capacity and local relief, with no $/MWh strike, no basis, and recruitment cycles measured in months instead of development years.

history.event: CalReady's first season: ~16,000 homes prove the model in statewide events.
Fleet quadruples to ~56,000 customers / 75,000 batteries, ~250 MW of two-hour dispatch capability.
PG&E SAVE / Local PeakShift Power dispatches 50+ times, 1,200+ dispatching hours of targeted local relief.

vppCases.lesson: When large-load requests exceed available grid capacity, distributed resources can add capacity faster than a new central plant. Contracting them means buying measured performance and dispatch rights, not output at one plant meter.
